title: The Reactance Lab
summary: Find the reactance and current of an inductor or capacitor, and see why they absorb no net power.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 7.4, AC voltage applied to an inductor
learningOutcome: The student can find the reactance and rms current of an inductor or capacitor, predict what a change of frequency does, and explain why they absorb no net power with the current 90° out of phase.

levels.title: The inductor
levels.adds: Baseline: X_L = ωL and I = V/X_L (Ex 7.3, Example 7.2).
hints: X_L = ωL with L in henry (mH × 10⁻³).

levels.title: The capacitor
levels.adds: New idea: X_C = 1/ωC, which falls as the frequency rises (Ex 7.4, Example 7.4).
hints: The capacitor opposes the current less at higher frequency.

levels.title: Change the frequency
levels.adds: Apply it: an inductor’s reactance rises with frequency and a capacitor’s falls, changing the lamp’s brightness (Examples 7.3, 7.5).
hints: X_L is proportional to f. X_C is proportional to 1/f.
A smaller reactance means a larger current.
A larger current makes the lamp glow brighter.

levels.title: No net power
levels.adds: New idea: the current lags the voltage in an inductor and leads it in a capacitor, and the average power is zero (Ex 7.5).
hints: The phase difference is 90°, so cos φ = 0.
Inductor: the current lags. Capacitor: the current leads.
The energy stored in a quarter cycle is returned in the next.

misconceptions: A capacitor blocks the current more at high frequency
An inductor absorbs power from an AC source
The current in an inductor leads the voltage
